lines.text: Here's a simpler rule: speed equals P, just a number, times the distance, capped at top speed.
Let's race it against ours, in our simulator.
Round one: P is five, with an acceleration limit of three meters per second squared.
The simple robot overshoots. In the worst runs, by about two meters.
Why? It only slows once P times d drops below its speed: at d equals v over P.
Four over five: it starts braking zero point eight meters out.
But stopping from four at three needs sixteen over six: two point six seven meters.
Round two: a limit of ten. Stopping takes zero point eight meters, exactly where it starts braking.
Zero margin. Any delay, and it slides past: twenty centimeters, in our simulator.
Round three: a gentle P of two. It brakes from two meters out and stops cleanly.
But its speed shrinks with distance, so it creeps in.
It reached five centimeters in two point two zero seconds. Ours: one point three nine.
So P alone must choose: fast and overshoot, or safe and slow.
Ours asks "can I still stop?", so from top speed it brakes at one point five three meters.
It plans six while the limit allows ten; the gentle line takes the last third of a meter.
Full speed for longer, no overshoot. All from one square root.
